questions.q: Why does Mara design three zones instead of just two (corporate IT and OT/SCADA)?
options: Three zones are required by a specific compliance standard

A direct boundary between corporate IT and OT/SCADA would force every legitimate access path to cross it directly, risking the same kind of broad general-allow rule that caused the Intermediate project's incident
Three zones are simply the default in every firewall vendor's documentation
Because Hartwell only has three network switches available
questions.explain: Introducing a narrow DMZ/jump zone means nothing in corporate IT ever talks to OT/SCADA directly, avoiding the broad 'it's needed sometimes, so allow it generally' pattern that caused the earlier incident.

questions.q: What is Zone 2 in this plan, and what is its one job?
options: A backup OT/SCADA zone in case Zone 3 fails
The DMZ/jump zone containing only hardened jump boxes — the only path allowed to initiate a connection into the OT/SCADA zone
A zone for guest Wi-Fi traffic
An extension of the corporate IT zone with slightly stricter rules
questions.explain: Zone 2 is a narrow DMZ/jump zone: the only permitted path into Zone 3, meaning nothing in Zone 1 (corporate IT) ever reaches OT/SCADA directly.

questions.q: In the Azure NSG rule set for the snet-scada-gateway subnet, why is an explicit low-priority Deny-All-Inbound rule added even though NSGs already deny by default?
options: It isn't necessary and was added by mistake
It makes the deny-by-default intent visible and auditable in every rule review, instead of depending on a reviewer remembering that an unlisted rule means denied
Azure NSGs allow everything by default, so this rule is required to deny anything at all
It improves network throughput
questions.explain: The explicit Deny-All-Inbound rule is a visible, auditable statement of intent — it shows up directly in every rule review rather than relying on an implicit, easy-to-overlook default.

questions.q: On the AWS side, how is the OT telemetry account's network boundary enforced?
options: By sharing a VPC with other corporate workloads for simplicity
A dedicated VPC, vpc-hartwell-scada, with AWS Network Firewall allowing inbound only from the jump zone's IP range on the required port, denying and logging everything else
By disabling networking entirely on that account
By relying solely on IAM policies, with no network-layer controls
questions.explain: The OT telemetry lives in its own dedicated VPC with a Network Firewall rule group mirroring the Azure design: allow only from the jump zone, deny and log everything else.

questions.q: Why does this lesson's plan get deployed in monitor-only mode before enforcement, in the next lesson?
options: Monitor-only mode is a permanent state and enforcement never actually happens
So Mara can see what traffic the new rules would have blocked before anything is actually blocked, catching a legitimate dependency before it causes an outage
Because the firewall hardware doesn't support enforcement mode yet
It's required by the vendor's warranty terms
questions.explain: Deploying in logging/monitor-only mode first surfaces what the rules would have blocked, so an unnoticed legitimate dependency can be caught and addressed before enforcement actually breaks it.
